text: SAVE CORAL GULLY, by marine scientist Dr Lena Moss. Coral Gully, on the northern side of Bluster Rock, is home to the island's last healthy patch of reef. In the past five years, our surveys have found that the number of fish on the reef has fallen by almost half. I believe the council should make Coral Gully a no-fishing sanctuary, where the reef can rest and recover. I know that many fishing families fear the sanctuary will leave their nets empty. At Pelican Point, catches just outside a sanctuary doubled within ten years of it opening. That happens because fish grow large and breed inside the protected area, then spill out into the water around it. Coral Gully has the island's last 300 giant clams, which have nearly vanished elsewhere. The council will decide at its meeting on the first Monday of next month. I urge every resident who cares about the reef to come along and speak up. Copies of our survey results are available at the library.

frame: Ada Pennick is drafting a second letter about the turtles. The Bilbolster is reading it from a rock pool.
text: Dear Editor, Last month, I wrote to object to jet ski hire in Bluster Bay, and many readers have asked me why I am so certain that jet skis are hurting the turtles. It is a fair question. The northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles for as long as anyone can remember, and every summer, volunteers like me count the nests, fence them off and watch the hatchlings scramble down to the water. Until this year, injured turtles were rare. Each nest holds around a hundred eggs, and the hatchlings come out at night, guided by the moonlight on the water. Jet skis are allowed in the bay from 7 am to 7 pm, seven days a week, and the hire shop has twelve of them. On a busy Saturday, all twelve are out on the water at once. I am not against fun, and I am not against tourists, who bring welcome money to our town. But I believe that jet skis are hurting the turtles, and I want to show readers why. I have one sentence left to write before I send this letter, and I want it to be the strongest backing I can give. The council will vote on the jet ski hire licence on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer

frame: The Bugle has printed an opinion piece about the music festival. The Kindalah is sorting it, feather by feather.
text: BRING BACK THE FESTIVAL: an opinion piece by Jojo Reyes of Red Dust Static. The Bluster Rock Music Festival has not been held since 2019, and I believe the council should bring it back next autumn. Some people say a festival is too noisy, too expensive and too much trouble for a small town. I understand those worries, and I don't want to pretend they aren't real. Like many people my age, I first heard live music at that festival, sitting on my dad's shoulders in the dust and watching a bush band play until midnight. Our band still has a faded festival T-shirt from that year, and our drummer wears it to every gig for luck. But I have spent the last month gathering backing for my claim that a festival would be good for Bluster Rock, and I think the case is strong. I spoke to shopkeepers, read the council's own reports, interviewed people who study tourism and music, and listened to locals who remember the old festivals. Below are six pieces of the backing I found. I hope that readers will judge each one on its merits. If the council agrees, three local bands have already offered to play for free, and the old flatbed truck behind the footy club could serve as a stage.

frame: Two texts describe the old Crowley homestead. One is a museum plaque; the other is a ghost tour flyer.
text: MUSEUM PLAQUE: The Crowley homestead was built from local sandstone in 1884 by Elsie and Tom Crowley, who ran sheep on the surrounding land for thirty years. The house has six rooms, a cellar and a stone water tank that still holds rain. After the family moved to the coast in 1914, the homestead stood empty until the island council lovingly restored it in 1998.
